10-minute-language-microsprints.title: Practice One Small Language Skill for a Short Session
10-minute-language-microsprints.description: Use a short study session to practice one narrow language skill such as recalling a few words, listening to a short clip, or speaking a brief response. Ten minutes is a convenient starting point, not a required dose.
10-minute-language-microsprints.reason: Replace an inherited language-study article containing invented adherence results, unsupported recall percentages, arbitrary targets and overconfident learning claims with a simple short-practice protocol.
forbidden_public_fragments: increased adherence in our small pilots from 62% to 82%
Research shows habits can take 21-66 days to form

lifeOsSource.hack: Choose one small language skill and practice it for a short session. Keep the target narrow enough to finish, then note what felt easy or difficult and choose the next practice.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Pick one narrow language task, such as reviewing a few phrases, listening to a short clip, reading a small passage, or recording a brief spoken answer. Practice for a short session and finish with one note about what to revisit next.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: What did I practice, what could I recall or understand without help, and what is the next small thing worth repeating?

faq.question: Does the session need to be ten minutes?
faq.answer: No. Ten minutes is simply an easy container for a short practice. Use a duration that fits your attention and the skill you are working on.

faq.question: What should I practice in a short session?
faq.answer: Choose one narrow task: recall a few words, repeat useful phrases, listen to a short clip, read a small passage, or record a brief spoken response. Avoid trying to cover every language skill at once.

faq.question: Is a short session enough to learn a language?
faq.answer: No single short session is enough by itself. The point is to make one useful practice manageable. Broader progress needs repeated exposure, practice, feedback, and more time across different skills.

intro.html: A short language session is useful when a larger study plan feels hard to start or when you want a small piece of practice inside a busy day. Keep the target narrow, do the practice, and leave yourself one clear next step.

sections.title: 1. Choose one small skill
sections.html: Pick one thing for this session: recall vocabulary, listen for a phrase, read a short passage, practise pronunciation, or answer one speaking prompt. A narrow target makes the session easier to finish and review.

sections.title: 2. Set a small session boundary
sections.html: Ten minutes is a convenient default if you need one. Shorter or longer is fine. The boundary is there to make starting easy, not to define how much language learning should happen in a day.

sections.title: 3. Do something with the language
sections.html: Whenever possible, include a small act of recall or production rather than only looking at material. Say the phrase, answer the question, write the sentence, or try to recall before checking the answer.

sections.title: 4. Keep the setup light
sections.html: Use the material you already have when possible. A short practice loses much of its value if most of the session is spent choosing an app, reorganizing a deck, or searching for the perfect resource.

sections.title: 5. Leave one next step
sections.html: Write down one phrase, error, sound, or question to revisit. This gives the next short session a starting point without creating another complicated study system.

sections.title: 6. Review whether short sessions help
sections.html: After several sessions, notice whether this format helps you practise more consistently and whether the tasks are challenging enough to matter. If not, change the duration, material, or skill focus.
